Quantum Tunneling: Instead of using heat (thermionic emission), a high voltage (extracting voltage) is applied to the tip. questions.question: What is a Supporting electrolyte in Polarography? / [CO5]
questions.solution_html: • What is a Supporting electrolyte in Polarography? [U] / [CO5] A supporting electrolyte is an inert electrolyte added in large excess to the analyte solution to increase its electrical conductivity and eliminate the migration current. It does not participate in the electrode reaction but helps maintain a constant ionic strength throughout the experiment. The supporting electrolyte ensures that the movement of electroactive species toward the electrode occurs mainly by diﬀusion rather than by migration under the inﬂuence of an electric ﬁeld. This improves the accuracy and shape of the polarographic wave. Common examples of supporting electrolytes include potassium chloride (KCl), potassium nitrate (KNO ₃ ), and sodium sulfate (Na ₂ SO ₄ ). (Deﬁnition :3marks; Explanation :4marks)

questions.question: Explain the working of a SEM with the aid of a labelled diagram. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html: • Explain the working of a SEM with the aid of a labeled diagram. [K] / [CO1] This technique provides high-resolution imaging and detailed information about the sample's surface topography and composition. Scanning Electron Microscopy works on the principle of the interaction between a focused beam of high-energy electrons and the surface of a specimen. In SEM, a beam of electrons is generated by an electron gun and focused onto the sample surface using electromagnetic lenses. When the electron beam strikes the specimen, various signals such as secondary electrons, backscattered electrons, and characteristic X-rays are produced due to electron–matter interactions. The emitted secondary electrons are collected by a detector and converted into electrical signals to form a highly magniﬁed image of the sample surface. Since the electron beam scans the specimen point by point, detailed information about the surface morphology, texture, composition, and topography of the material can be obtained. Key Principles of SEM a). Electron Beam Generation and Focusing, b). Scanning and Interaction c). Signal Detection and Image Formation (Working Principle-4 marks, Labelled diagram -3 marks)
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Explain the working principle of AFM. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html: • Explain the working principle of AFM. [U] / [CO2] Atomic Force Microscope can analyze conducting as well as non-conducting materials and provides detailed information about surface morphology, roughness, and nanoscale structures with atomic-level resolution. It works on the principle of measuring the force of interaction between a sharp probe tip and the surface of a sample. In AFM, a very ﬁne tip attached to a ﬂexible cantilever scans across the surface of the specimen. As the tip moves over the sample, attractive or repulsive forces between the atoms of the tip and the sample cause the cantilever to bend or deﬂect. A laser beam is focused onto the back of the cantilever, and the reﬂected beam falls on a photodetector. The deﬂection of the cantilever changes the position of the reﬂected laser beam, which is converted into electrical signals. These signals are processed by a computer to generate a high-resolution three-dimensional image of the surface. (Working Principle-4 marks, Any schematic diagram -3 marks)

questions.question: Explain the basic principle of Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS). Discuss the two primary mechanisms responsible for the signal enhancement and mention two practical applications in nanotechnology. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html: • Explain the basic principle of Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS). Discuss the two primary mechanisms responsible for the signal enhancement. [An] / [CO3] Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (SERS): Amplifies signals by factors of 10 6 to 10 11 using localized electromagnetic fields on metallic nanostructures. SERS addresses the primary limitation of standard Raman spectroscopy—its extremely low scattering cross-section. Mechanisms involved in SERS (a) Electromagnetic Mechanism (EM) is the dominant contributor to signal enhancement. It occurs when the incident laser frequency matches the Localized Surface Plasmon Resonances (LSPR) of noble metal nanostructures (like gold or silver). This creates a massive local electric field, and the resulting Raman intensity scales approximately with the fourth power of this field enhancement. (b) A secondary effect providing a smaller boost (factors of 10 1 to 10 3 ), which involves charge-transfer processes between the metal surface and the adsorbed molecule, effectively acting as a resonance Raman effect. (c) Hot Spots: These are highly localized regions, such as the nanometric gaps between adjacent particles or sharp metallic tips, where the electromagnetic field and signal enhancement are exponentially higher than on flat surfaces. (Definition: 3 marks; Mechanisms: Each explanation contains 2 marks)

questions.question: Discuss the working principle of X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. Also explain how is it useful for quantitative elemental analysis. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the working principle of X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. Also explain how it is useful for quantitative elemental analysis. [U] / [CO3] X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), also known as Electron Spectroscopy for Chemical Analysis (ESCA) is a widely used technique to investigate the chemical composition of the surfaces. Working Principle XPS is based on the photoelectric effect. When a sample is bombarded with a beam of monochromatic X-rays, the X-ray photons interact with the inner-shell electrons of the atoms in the sample. Usually an Aluminum or Magnesium anode is used as the X-ray Source. If the energy of the X-ray photon hv is greater than the binding energy (BE)of an electron, the electron is ejected from the atom as a photoelectron. The kinetic energy of these emitted photoelectrons is measured using an electron spectrometer. The binding energy of the electron, which is characteristic of the element and its orbital, can be calculated by Koopman's theorem. KE = hv
  • - BE
  • - φ Where:BE= Electron Binding Energy, KE= Electron Kinetic Energy, φ= Spectrometer Work Function Because each element has a unique set of binding energies, the resulting spectrum of intensity versus binding energy allows for the identification of all elements (except hydrogen and helium) present on the surface. The kinetic energy difference between the peak of the sample and corresponding peak in a reference compound is known as chemical shift.The shifts of the photoelectron lines in an ESCA spectrum reflect the increase in binding energy. ESCA chemical shifts lie in the range 0-1500eV. questions.question: Describe the basic intrumental features of FESEM with a schematic diagram. / [CO1] [15x1 = 15]
questions.solution_html: • Describe the basic instrumental features of FESEM with a schematic diagram. [U] / [CO1] The fundamental principle of FESEM (Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy) lies in its unique method of generating electrons. While a standard SEM uses heat to "boil" electrons oﬀ a ﬁlament, FESEM uses a powerful electric ﬁeld to pull them from a sharp needle-like tip. This results in a beam that is much thinner, more coherent, and signiﬁcantly higher in brightness, allowing for ultra-high-resolution imaging down to 1 nanometer .
